item.content:encoded:
I like this new version. That is, despite the moment of odd redaction. I mean, "SCP-390 may in fact have been [DATA EXPUNGED]"? Come on Foundation, we all know this is Archimedes' fabled Death Ray weapon. It's obvious.

In fact, I'd argue that this article functions as an inversion of the usual Archimedes-legend, and only works when in conjunction with knowledge of that background. Everything Archimedean is turned on its head. We thought of him as a forefather to modern science; turns out his invention broke all of our laws of physics. The "death ray" story (if you believe the Mythbusters' results) is supposed to be a myth, a piece of pure fantasy tackled onto his list of inventions; turns out? Fully armed and operational, baby. History records several variations on how Archimedes died, all portray it as a tragic lost for the whole of Humanity. Turns out, Archimedes dying is the greatest boon ever imagined.

tl;dr: +1

item.content:encoded:
I'm a big fan of Out Of Place Artifacts. The Antikythera Mechanism, ancient Greek automata, that kind of stuff. That said, this is really damn bare bones. The Archimedian heat ray, if it actually existed, was used at the Siege of Syracuse, the same siege where Archimedes died at the hands of a Roman soldier, despite the commands of General Marcellus. Why not make the heat ray the reason he was killed? The soldier saw the destruction it caused, and killed Archie to stop him from building any more.

Hell, legend stated that Archimedes used the shields of the Roman soldiers to create a heat ray to ignite the ships, but that's since been proven impossible thanks to Mythbusters. What if these devices were in the shields used by the Roman forces, and that's how he did it, but it was explained away as being a reflective effect? Archimedes knew it was impossible, so he just built a fucking laser so he wouldn't look stupid when the Romans did it.

Just my two cents.

item.title: Staff Post
item.content:encoded:
This article is up for review. Check it out, it needs more attention!

This really feels like an article where everything you need to know about it is summarized by the title. It's an ancient military laser. We found it in [DATA EXPUNGED] and restored it. To be honest, this doesn't really tell enough information to know whether it's anomalous or not. We never really get a detailed view of how this thing functions, anomalously or not, which strips this of what should be the most interesting component. And if this is supposed to be the Archimedes Heat Ray, than that aspect is pretty tacked on. The article doesn't make any good use of the inventor or the source material besides just telling the most basic, predictable version it can. It frustrates me, because I can see so much potential in this! I really can! But there's just nothing interesting about this article.

item.content:encoded: Mythbusters busted Archimedes' Death Ray, actually. Sorry to burst your bubble.

Boooring. The article's written pretty well, I think, nothing to object. It's the very idea of it to be boring, I guess: an ancient but technologically advanced weapon? Meh. Not a very bad idea, but you could arrange something more original and supernatural than "lasers". Plus, some kind of lasers actually existed in ancient Greece: large, circular, concave mirrors which reflected and focused solar rays upon ships and set them on fire. This means that not only it's not very interesting (in which case I would just have left no vote), but also it's neither very anomalous itself, nor historically plausible (who needs super-duper-complex machinery when you've got something equally effective, but far less difficult to create, build or understand?).1
No mirror has been armed during the production of this post.

Footnotes
1. Tl;dr version: Atlantidean weapons ought to be far more Atlantidean to impress me.

item.content:encoded:
Seeing as a lot of people still have no clue what the reference is:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes#The_Archimedes_Heat_Ray_.E2.80.93_myth_or_reality.3F

Archimedes lived from 287 BC to 212 BC, and was considered one of the leading scientists and inventors of antiquity, and an easy target of alien conspiracy theorists because of the revolutionary inventions he created.

During the Siege of Syracuse in 214-212 BC by the Roman Republic, it is said that Archimedes built several amazing devices to help the defenders of the city, including a "Heat Ray" or "Burning Glass" that could set enemy ships on fire from a long distance.

Historians have debated for a long time whether there's any credibility to this claim, and while Mythbusters considered this one 'busted' and impractical, this is an attempt to show that there is something 'off' with the whole thing. Lasers have only been around for a few decades, and have yet to even be put to use in actual military action, but somehow one was built over two millennia ago.
